title: Polar Coordinates and Conversions

sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Convert each polar point $(r, \theta)$ to rectangular coordinates (exact values):
Convert each rectangular point to polar coordinates with $r \geq 0$ and $0 \leq \theta < 2\pi$:
questions.answer: (a) $\left(3\sqrt{2}, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right)$; (b) $\left(5, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$
questions.explanation: (a) $\left(3\sqrt{2}, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right)$; (b) $\left(5, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$

questions.q: Convert the polar equation $r = 6\cos\theta$ to rectangular form and identify the curve.
questions.answer: Multiply by $r$: $r^2 = 6r\cos\theta$, so $x^2 + y^2 = 6x$, i.e. $(x - 3)^2 + y^2 = 9$: a circle with center $(3, 0)$ and radius 3.
questions.explanation: Multiply by $r$: $r^2 = 6r\cos\theta$, so $x^2 + y^2 = 6x$, i.e. $(x - 3)^2 + y^2 = 9$: a circle with center $(3, 0)$ and radius 3.

questions.q: Convert each rectangular equation to polar form:
questions.answer: (a) $r = 4$; (b) $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$
questions.explanation: (a) $r = 4$; (b) $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$

questions.q: Convert the polar equation $r = \frac{2}{1 - \sin\theta}$ to rectangular form.
questions.answer: $r - r\sin\theta = 2$, so $r = y + 2$. Squaring: $x^2 + y^2 = (y + 2)^2 = y^2 + 4y + 4$, so $x^2 = 4y + 4$ — a parabola.
questions.explanation: $r - r\sin\theta = 2$, so $r = y + 2$. Squaring: $x^2 + y^2 = (y + 2)^2 = y^2 + 4y + 4$, so $x^2 = 4y + 4$ — a parabola.

questions.q: Give two other pairs $(r,\theta)$ that represent the same point as $\left(3, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$: one with $r>0$ and $\theta$ outside $[0,2\pi)$, and one with $r<0$.
questions.answer: Adding a full rotation: $\left(3, \frac{\pi}{4}+2\pi\right) = \left(3,\frac{9\pi}{4}\right)$. Using negative $r$ (add $\pi$ to the angle): $\left(-3, \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi\right) = \left(-3,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)$.
questions.explanation: Adding a full rotation: $\left(3, \frac{\pi}{4}+2\pi\right) = \left(3,\frac{9\pi}{4}\right)$. Using negative $r$ (add $\pi$ to the angle): $\left(-3, \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi\right) = \left(-3,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)$.

questions.q: Plot-reasoning: explain why the polar point $\left(-2, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ corresponds to the same location as $\left(2, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$.
questions.answer: A negative $r$ means the point lies in the direction opposite to $\theta$. Pointing at angle $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (straight up) with $r=-2$ places the point 2 units in the opposite direction, straight down — the same location as $r=2$ at angle $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ (also straight down).
questions.explanation: A negative $r$ means the point lies in the direction opposite to $\theta$. Pointing at angle $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (straight up) with $r=-2$ places the point 2 units in the opposite direction, straight down — the same location as $r=2$ at angle $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ (also straight down).

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Convert $\left(4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$ and $\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ to rectangular coordinates, then find the distance between them, to two decimal places.
questions.answer: $\left(4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \rightarrow (2\sqrt{3}, 2)$; $\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) \rightarrow (-2, 2\sqrt{3})$. Distance $=\sqrt{(2\sqrt{3}+2)^2+(2-2\sqrt{3})^2} \approx \sqrt{29.86+2.14} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66$.
questions.explanation: $\left(4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \rightarrow (2\sqrt{3}, 2)$; $\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) \rightarrow (-2, 2\sqrt{3})$. Distance $=\sqrt{(2\sqrt{3}+2)^2+(2-2\sqrt{3})^2} \approx \sqrt{29.86+2.14} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66$.

questions.q: Convert each polar point to rectangular coordinates (exact values):
Convert the polar equation $r^2 = 4\sin2\theta$ to note its symmetry, and identify it as a standard curve type.
questions.answer: This is a lemniscate (figure-eight curve). Rewriting $r^2=4\sin2\theta = 8\sin\theta\cos\theta$, and using $r^2=x^2+y^2$, $r\cos\theta=x$, $r\sin\theta=y$: multiplying both sides by $r^2$ gives $(x^2+y^2)^2 = 8xy$.
questions.explanation: This is a lemniscate (figure-eight curve). Rewriting $r^2=4\sin2\theta = 8\sin\theta\cos\theta$, and using $r^2=x^2+y^2$, $r\cos\theta=x$, $r\sin\theta=y$: multiplying both sides by $r^2$ gives $(x^2+y^2)^2 = 8xy$.

questions.q: Explain why, unlike rectangular coordinates, a single point can be represented by infinitely many polar coordinate pairs.
questions.target: Why polar coordinates are not unique
questions.answer: Adding any multiple of $2\pi$ to $\theta$ returns to the same direction, and reversing the sign of $r$ while adding $\pi$ to $\theta$ also gives the same point — so every point has infinitely many valid $(r,\theta)$ representations, unlike the one-to-one rectangular system.
questions.explanation: Adding any multiple of $2\pi$ to $\theta$ returns to the same direction, and reversing the sign of $r$ while adding $\pi$ to $\theta$ also gives the same point — so every point has infinitely many valid $(r,\theta)$ representations, unlike the one-to-one rectangular system.

questions.q: The pole (origin) is a special case in polar coordinates. Explain why.
questions.target: Why polar coordinates are not unique
questions.answer: The pole corresponds to $r=0$ for ANY value of $\theta$ — every angle gives the same point (the origin) when $r=0$, so the pole has no single well-defined angle.
questions.explanation: The pole corresponds to $r=0$ for ANY value of $\theta$ — every angle gives the same point (the origin) when $r=0$, so the pole has no single well-defined angle.

questions.q: Convert the rectangular equation $x^2-y^2=4$ (a hyperbola) to polar form.
questions.answer: $r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta=4 \Rightarrow r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=4 \Rightarrow r^2\cos(2\theta)=4$.
questions.explanation: $r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta=4 \Rightarrow r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=4 \Rightarrow r^2\cos(2\theta)=4$.

questions.q: Convert the polar point $\left(-4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$ (negative $r$) to rectangular coordinates.
questions.target: More point conversions with negative r
questions.answer: $x=r\cos\theta=-4\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=-2\sqrt{3}$. $y=r\sin\theta=-4\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{1}{2}=-2$. Point: $(-2\sqrt{3},-2)$.
questions.explanation: $x=r\cos\theta=-4\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=-2\sqrt{3}$. $y=r\sin\theta=-4\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{1}{2}=-2$. Point: $(-2\sqrt{3},-2)$.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Convert the rectangular point $(-4,-4)$ to polar coordinates with $r>0$ and $0\leq\theta<2\pi$.
questions.target: More point conversions with negative r
questions.answer: $r=\sqrt{16+16}=4\sqrt{2}$. Both coordinates negative places this in QIII, reference angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$: $\theta=\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{5\pi}{4}$.
questions.explanation: $r=\sqrt{16+16}=4\sqrt{2}$. Both coordinates negative places this in QIII, reference angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$: $\theta=\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{5\pi}{4}$.

questions.q: The Archimedean spiral $r=\theta$ has no simple rectangular equivalent, but explain qualitatively why it spirals outward as $\theta$ increases.
questions.answer: Since $r=\theta$, the radius grows in direct proportion to the angle swept — each additional full rotation ($2\pi$ radians) pushes $r$ out by $2\pi$ more units, producing evenly-spaced spiral arms rather than a closed curve.
questions.explanation: Since $r=\theta$, the radius grows in direct proportion to the angle swept — each additional full rotation ($2\pi$ radians) pushes $r$ out by $2\pi$ more units, producing evenly-spaced spiral arms rather than a closed curve.

questions.q: A radar station models detected objects using polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ where $r$ is distance in km and $\theta$ is bearing angle. An aircraft is detected at $(r,\theta)=(45,\frac{5\pi}{6})$. Convert this to rectangular coordinates (kilometers east and north of the station), to two decimal places.
questions.cross_lesson: 2.03 Graphs of Sine and Cosine Functions
questions.answer: $x=45\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}=45\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\approx-38.97$ km. $y=45\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=45\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=22.50$ km. The aircraft is about $38.97$ km west and $22.50$ km north of the station.
questions.explanation: $x=45\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}=45\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\approx-38.97$ km. $y=45\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=45\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=22.50$ km. The aircraft is about $38.97$ km west and $22.50$ km north of the station.

questions.q: A second aircraft is detected at rectangular coordinates $(30,-40)$ relative to the same radar station. Convert to polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ with $r>0$ and $0\leq\theta<2\pi$, to two decimal places.
questions.cross_lesson: 2.04 Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
questions.answer: $r=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=\sqrt{900+1600}=\sqrt{2500}=50$ km. Reference angle $=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{40}{30}\right)\approx53.13°\approx0.93$ rad. Since $x>0,y<0$ (QIV): $\theta\approx2\pi-0.93\approx5.35$ rad.
questions.explanation: $r=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=\sqrt{900+1600}=\sqrt{2500}=50$ km. Reference angle $=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{40}{30}\right)\approx53.13°\approx0.93$ rad. Since $x>0,y<0$ (QIV): $\theta\approx2\pi-0.93\approx5.35$ rad.

questions.q: Convert the rectangular equation of a vertical line, $x=5$, to polar form, and explain why the result is not simply a constant $r$.
questions.cross_lesson: 3.01 The Unit Circle and Exact Values
questions.answer: $r\cos\theta=5 \Rightarrow r=\frac{5}{\cos\theta}=5\sec\theta$. Unlike a circle centered at the pole (constant $r$), a vertical line's distance from the pole varies with direction $\theta$, so $r$ must depend on $\theta$ through the secant function.
questions.explanation: $r\cos\theta=5 \Rightarrow r=\frac{5}{\cos\theta}=5\sec\theta$. Unlike a circle centered at the pole (constant $r$), a vertical line's distance from the pole varies with direction $\theta$, so $r$ must depend on $\theta$ through the secant function.

questions.q: Convert the polar equation $r=6$ to rectangular form, and explain in one sentence why this equation contains no $\theta$ term.
questions.answer: $x^2+y^2=36$ (squaring both sides of $r=6$). There is no $\theta$ term because every direction from the pole at distance $6$ satisfies the equation equally — the curve is a full circle, independent of angle.
questions.explanation: $x^2+y^2=36$ (squaring both sides of $r=6$). There is no $\theta$ term because every direction from the pole at distance $6$ satisfies the equation equally — the curve is a full circle, independent of angle.

sections.heading: Part IV — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Foundational Concept Mastery (21–28)

questions.q: How is a point with negative radius $(-r, \theta)$ plotted in polar coordinates?
questions.target: Plotting with Positive and Negative Radii
choices: Plot along the opposite ray directly across the pole (angle $\theta + \pi$)
questions.answer: A negative radius $-r$ means moving a distance $r$ backward along the line passing through angle $\theta$, which lands at $(r, \theta + \pi)$.
questions.explanation: A negative radius $-r$ means moving a distance $r$ backward along the line passing through angle $\theta$, which lands at $(r, \theta + \pi)$.

questions.q: Which polar coordinate represents the same point as $(3, \pi/3)$?
questions.target: Plotting with Positive and Negative Radii
questions.answer: Adding $\pi$ to the angle and negating the radius gives $(-3, \pi/3 + \pi) = (-3, 4\pi/3)$.
questions.explanation: Adding $\pi$ to the angle and negating the radius gives $(-3, \pi/3 + \pi) = (-3, 4\pi/3)$.

questions.q: In which quadrant does the polar point $(4, 7\pi/6)$ lie?
questions.target: Plotting with Positive and Negative Radii
questions.answer: Angle $7\pi/6 = 210^\circ$ lies in Quadrant III. With positive radius $r = 4$, the point is in Quadrant III.
questions.explanation: Angle $7\pi/6 = 210^\circ$ lies in Quadrant III. With positive radius $r = 4$, the point is in Quadrant III.

questions.q: State the formulas to convert polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ to Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$.
questions.answer: By standard right-triangle trigonometry, $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$.
questions.explanation: By standard right-triangle trigonometry, $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$.

questions.q: Convert the polar point $(6, 2\pi/3)$ to exact Cartesian coordinates.
Convert $(4, -\pi/4)$ to Cartesian coordinates.
Convert the Cartesian point $(-2, 2)$ to polar coordinates with $r > 0$ and $0 \leq \theta < 2\pi$.
questions.answer: $r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$. In Quadrant II, $\theta = 3\pi/4$.
questions.explanation: $r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$. In Quadrant II, $\theta = 3\pi/4$.

questions.q: Convert $(0, -5)$ to polar coordinates.
questions.answer: Distance $r = 5$. The point lies on the negative $y$-axis, which is angle $\theta = 3\pi/2$.
questions.explanation: Distance $r = 5$. The point lies on the negative $y$-axis, which is angle $\theta = 3\pi/2$.

questions.q: Convert $(3, -3\sqrt{3})$ to polar coordinates with $r > 0$ and $0 \leq \theta < 2\pi$.
questions.answer: $r = \sqrt{9 + 27} = \sqrt{36} = 6$. In Quadrant IV with $\tan\theta = -\sqrt{3}$, $\theta = 2\pi - \pi/3 = 5\pi/3$.
questions.explanation: $r = \sqrt{9 + 27} = \sqrt{36} = 6$. In Quadrant IV with $\tan\theta = -\sqrt{3}$, $\theta = 2\pi - \pi/3 = 5\pi/3$.

questions.q: Convert the polar equation $r = 4\cos\theta$ to Cartesian form.
questions.target: Converting Equations Between Polar and Cartesian
questions.answer: Multiply by $r$: $r^2 = 4r\cos\theta \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 4x \Rightarrow (x - 2)^2 + y^2 = 4$.
questions.explanation: Multiply by $r$: $r^2 = 4r\cos\theta \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 4x \Rightarrow (x - 2)^2 + y^2 = 4$.

questions.q: Convert $r = 5\csc\theta$ to Cartesian form.
questions.target: Converting Equations Between Polar and Cartesian
questions.answer: $r = \frac{5}{\sin\theta} \Rightarrow r\sin\theta = 5 \Rightarrow y = 5$.
questions.explanation: $r = \frac{5}{\sin\theta} \Rightarrow r\sin\theta = 5 \Rightarrow y = 5$.

questions.q: Convert the line $y = 3x$ to a polar equation.
questions.target: Converting Equations Between Polar and Cartesian
questions.answer: Substitute $x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta$: $r\sin\theta = 3r\cos\theta \Rightarrow \tan\theta = 3 \Rightarrow \theta = \arctan(3)$.
questions.explanation: Substitute $x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta$: $r\sin\theta = 3r\cos\theta \Rightarrow \tan\theta = 3 \Rightarrow \theta = \arctan(3)$.

questions.q: A complex number is represented by the point $P(3, 4)$ in the complex plane. What is the modulus of this complex number?
questions.answer: The complex number can be written as $z = 3 + 4i$. The modulus of a complex number $z = a + bi$ is given by $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. In this case, $a = 3$ and $b = 4$. Therefore, the modulus is $|z| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.
questions.explanation: The complex number can be written as $z = 3 + 4i$. The modulus of a complex number $z = a + bi$ is given by $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. In this case, $a = 3$ and $b = 4$. Therefore, the modulus is $|z| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.
